rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 describe a 2021 field experiment at Shihezi, Xinjiang, with aerated vs non-aerated drip irrigation and two N rates on processing tomato, three replicates. Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 3 report that aerated irrigation increased yield, YPP, IWUE and NPFP, with A1N2 yielding 32.05 t/ha, 23.69% above A0N1; aeration effect on yield highly significant (p<0.01). Q4: Section 3.5 and Figure 8 present a path analysis in which fertilizer-air coupled drip irrigation alters soil nutrients (measured in Fig. 4) and C/N cycling gene abundance (Fig. 5), which in turn directly affect yield (NO3-N direct path coefficient -1.047, C cycling genes 0.924). Q9: Table 3 reports yield, YPP, SFW, NFPP, IWUE and NPFP as mean <U+00B1> standard deviation (n=3).
rows.notes: Study supports only the yield part of the passage; crop quality, pesticide reduction and nutrient over-consumption were not measured. Q3: yield measured by one harvest method only. Q4 answered yes on the basis of the path analysis via measured soil nutrients and gene abundance; the root-zone oxygen mechanism itself was not measured. Q5/Q6: single site, single crop, single season, plot scale (15 m x 1.45 m). Q7: authors recommend combining aeration with moderate N but do not state it as a requirement; aeration raised yield at both N levels. Q8: no limitations of the result stated.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 describe a 2021 field experiment with aerated vs non-aerated drip irrigation and two N rates on processing tomato in Xinjiang.
rows.notes: The study does not measure pesticide use, pest or disease incidence; Section 2.2 states weeding and pesticide applications were applied uniformly across all plots as standard practice. It reports yield, soil nutrients, GHG emissions and C/N cycling gene abundance only, so there is no own evidence on reduced pesticide applications.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 describe a 2021 replicated field experiment at Shihezi, Xinjiang, comparing aerated and non-aerated drip irrigation at two N rates on processing tomato. Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 3 show aerated irrigation increased fruit weight, yield per plant, total yield, IWUE and NPFP (p<0.01), with A1N2 highest at 32.05 t/ha, 23.69% above A0N1. Q4: Section 3.5 and Figure 8 path analysis link the irrigation treatment to yield via measured soil nutrients (Fig. 4) and C/N cycling gene abundance (Fig. 5), with NO3-N and C cycling genes having the largest direct effects on yield. Q9: Table 3 gives yield and components as mean <U+00B1> SD (n=3).
rows.notes: Q3: single method (harvest yield). Q4 yes on the basis of the path analysis through measured intermediate soil variables, although soil oxygen/aeration itself was not measured. Q5/Q6: one site, one crop, one season, plot scale. Q7: combination with moderate N is recommended but not stated as a necessary condition. Q8: no limitations stated.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 describe a 2021 replicated field experiment with aerated vs non-aerated drip irrigation on processing tomato in Xinjiang. Q2: Section 3.1 and Figure 4 report that aeration increased SOC and DOC (by 1.75-10.94% and 3.21-3.30%) and NH4+-N (7.75-14.44%) in the 0-40 cm layer compared with non-aerated drip; abstract states aerated irrigation increased SOC, DOC, TN and NH4+-N. Q9: Figure 4 caption states bars represent the standard deviation of the mean (n=3).
rows.notes: Evidence on soil condition is mixed: Section 3.1 also reports aeration reduced TN and NO3-N by 11.39% and 20.00%, and Section 3.3 reports aeration increased N2O, CH4, CO2 and total GHG emissions. Q3: single soil sampling and laboratory method. Q4: the mechanism (improved root-zone aeration stimulating microbial activity) is asserted in the Discussion, not measured; gene abundance was measured but not shown as the pathway from aeration to nutrient change. Q5/Q6: single sandy loam site, one crop, one season, plot scale. Q7/Q8: no required conditions or limitations stated for the soil result.

notes: Full text appears complete. Single-season (2021), single-site field trial on processing tomato under plastic-mulched drip with Venturi aeration; soil and gene sampling at a single date (end of fruit expansion). Minor internal inconsistencies (abstract says aeration increased TN while results say it reduced TN; discussion refers to 240 kg/ha N for A1N2 while treatments used 270 kg/ha).
